title: Leadership Supervision and Programme Management
reference_framework: NASW/ASWB supervision standards; IFSW ethical principles

modules.title: Leadership governance and role clarity
modules.outcome: Clarify decision authority, conflicts of interest and accountability in programme teams.

teaching_points.text: Delegation should state the decision scope, constraints, support and escalation route; it is not unlimited transfer of responsibility.
When personal interests could influence a decision, disclose the conflict and use the organisation's independent decision process.
Record the decision, its reasons, authority, owner and review point; minutes that only say 'agreed' do not establish accountability.
Invite relevant perspectives before decisions and explain how disagreement was handled; inclusion is more than unanimous-looking minutes.
Authority to manage a programme does not automatically confer competence or permission to perform specialist professional tasks.

modules.title: Reflective supervision and team support
modules.outcome: Use structured supervision to support learning, wellbeing and safe escalation.

teaching_points.text: A supervision agreement should clarify purpose, roles, regularity, records, confidentiality limits and routes for urgent concerns.
Reflective supervision explores observations, assumptions, emotions and alternatives, then agrees a learning action; it is more than checking task counts.
Supportive supervision does not replace urgent safeguarding or incident procedures; use the appropriate route without waiting for a scheduled session.
Feedback should identify specific behaviour and its effect, invite the worker's perspective, and agree a feasible improvement and review.
Repeated overload is a work-design issue to review as well as an individual support concern; consider case demands, resources and safe priorities.

modules.title: Programme management and learning
modules.outcome: Use delivery information to manage risks, resources and authorised programme adjustments.

teaching_points.text: Track an implementation issue with its impact, owner, action and review date; a list without follow-up is not a management response.
A variance from plan should be explained before action: compare intended and actual delivery, investigate causes and consider service effects.
Changes beyond delegated limits require approval; document why a change is proposed and its likely effects before committing resources.
Distinguish a delivery count from a result for participants; both can be useful but they answer different questions.
A learning adjustment should state the change, owner, expected effect and review criteria, while preserving safety and authorised scope.

questions.question: A coordinator tells a new worker to 'handle the whole project' without defining authority. What is the first governance improvement?

options.text: Assume the worker can sign every contract
Agree which decisions the worker can make and which require approval or escalation
Judge the worker only after the project ends
Remove all supervision to demonstrate trust

questions.rationale: Clear authority reduces ambiguity and supports appropriate decisions; vague delegation does not establish permission for every action.

questions.question: A manager is choosing a supplier owned by a close relative. What is the best next step?

options.text: Ask the relative to offer a personal reward
Omit the relationship from the decision record
Declare the conflict and follow the procurement and recusal process
Approve the supplier privately because it may be faster

questions.rationale: Disclosure and independent handling protect the decision process. A potentially useful supplier does not remove the conflict.

questions.question: A team cannot explain why it changed a service schedule. Which record would have helped most?

options.text: Only the total meeting duration
Only a list of attendees' favourite options
The reason, authorised decision, responsible owner and review date
Only the manager's job title

questions.rationale: A decision record connects the choice to its basis and follow-up, not merely to who was present.

questions.question: Frontline workers raise workload concerns but meeting minutes record only management's preferred option. What should the team improve?

options.text: Require workers to agree before they can speak
Stop inviting frontline workers
Delete the concerns to preserve a positive tone
Record and examine the concerns and explain the final decision

questions.rationale: A defensible process can reach a decision despite disagreement while retaining and responding to relevant evidence.

questions.question: A programme lead is asked to provide specialist clinical advice outside their training. What should they do?

options.text: Use an online summary as a substitute for competence
Recognise the limit and arrange appropriate qualified support through the agreed route
Ask a junior worker to give it under the lead's name
Give the advice because they manage the budget

questions.rationale: Management responsibility does not establish specialist competence. Appropriate consultation or referral protects role boundaries.

questions.question: A supervisee believes everything said in supervision is absolutely secret. What should the supervisor clarify?

options.text: That keeping no record removes every confidentiality issue
The agreement's confidentiality limits and how safety or other reportable concerns are handled
That no concern can ever leave the room
That all discussions will be posted publicly

questions.rationale: Supervision needs clear expectations. Neither absolute secrecy nor indiscriminate disclosure is an appropriate default.

questions.question: A worker says, 'I assumed the family was unwilling because they missed two appointments.' Which prompt best encourages reflection?

options.text: What evidence supports that view, what alternatives are possible, and how could you check them?
Which colleague can be blamed for the missed appointments?
Can you repeat the assumption in stronger language?
How can you close the case before the end of the day?

questions.rationale: The prompt separates evidence from interpretation and opens a practical learning step rather than reinforcing an untested judgement.

questions.question: A worker reports an immediate safeguarding concern shortly before a routine supervision meeting next week. What should the supervisor advise?

options.text: Use the applicable urgent safeguarding route now and arrange support alongside it
Save the concern for next week's reflective discussion
Treat a supportive conversation as completion of all required action
Ask the worker to keep it off the record

questions.rationale: Reflection and support are valuable but do not substitute for timely action through the appropriate safety procedure.

questions.question: A supervisor wants to address incomplete handovers. Which feedback is most useful?

options.text: Discuss a specific missing handover detail, its effect and an agreed improvement
Avoid feedback until the annual review
Compare the worker's personality with a colleague's
Tell the worker they are generally careless

questions.rationale: Specific, actionable feedback supports learning and follow-up; personal labels do not explain what should change.

questions.question: Several workers miss breaks and report growing backlogs. What is the best supervisory response?

options.text: Offer a wellbeing poster while leaving all demands unchanged
Treat every backlog as proof of poor motivation
Cancel supervision until the backlog disappears
Review workload and resources, agree safe priorities and offer support

questions.rationale: Support should address the conditions contributing to overload, not only encourage individuals to cope.

questions.question: A referral partner repeatedly misses agreed handovers. What should the programme lead record and act on?

options.text: Only the partner's logo
Only the original launch announcement
A note to discuss it at an unspecified future time
The effect on service continuity, responsible contacts and a dated corrective action

questions.rationale: A clear owner and follow-up make the issue actionable and connect it to service continuity.

questions.question: A programme is spending less than planned because accessible transport has not been provided. How should the lead interpret the underspend?

options.text: As permission to remove the transport budget permanently
As a possible delivery gap requiring investigation, not automatically as success
As irrelevant because the accounts balance
As proof that the service became more efficient

questions.rationale: Lower spending may reflect unmet service needs. Financial totals must be interpreted with delivery information.

questions.question: A coordinator wants to move funds to a new activity outside their delegated authority. What should happen first?

options.text: Submit the reason and implications through the authorised change process
Describe the new activity under the old budget label
Ask a supplier to hide the change in an invoice
Commit the money and request approval at year end

questions.rationale: The proposed change needs proper authority and a transparent record; relabelling does not create permission.

questions.question: A report says 200 sessions were delivered and therefore every participant's wellbeing improved. What is the problem?

options.text: The number is too small to report without doubling it
Delivery and outcomes must always be numerically identical
The session count does not by itself establish a participant outcome
A session count can never be recorded

questions.rationale: Delivery volume describes activity. The outcome claim needs appropriate evidence beyond the count.

questions.question: A pilot team changes appointment reminders after feedback. What makes this an accountable learning adjustment?

options.text: Remove unsuccessful participants from subsequent reporting
Change several unrelated processes without recording them
Document the change and owner, check risks, and agree how and when to review its effects
Assume every suggestion must be implemented permanently

questions.rationale: A bounded, documented change can be assessed and revised; unrecorded changes make learning and accountability harder.
